lessons.title: Cache coherence (MESI) and false sharing
lessons.summary: How multicore CPUs keep private caches in agreement, the MESI protocol and its MOESI/MESIF variants, snooping vs directories, what coherence costs, and how false sharing silently destroys multithreaded performance.
lessons.body:
Many multicore CPUs have private per-core caches, though which levels are private or shared depends on the design. If two cores both cache the line holding variable `x`, and one of them writes `x`, the other now holds a stale copy. Without a fix, two threads could see different values for the same address forever.

Within a hardware-coherent domain, **cache coherence** makes participating caches agree on a per-location write order. This does not make unsynchronised C/C++ data races valid, order accesses to different locations, or guarantee coherence with every device or memory type. Software still needs the language's atomics/synchronisation and any required device cache maintenance.

## The invariant

Coherence protocols maintain one rule per cache line:

> [!note] Single writer, multiple readers
> In a stable state, a line can have **one cache with exclusive write permission** (which can also read), or **multiple read-only cached copies**. It must not have a writable copy alongside independently usable shared copies.

In the **write-invalidate** protocol studied here, a writer must obtain exclusive permission and invalidate other usable copies. Write-update protocols instead distribute new data; their traffic trade-offs differ.

Note that coherence is about **one location**. The ordering rules across *different* locations are the **memory consistency model** (x86-TSO, Arm's weaker model), covered in the Parallel Hardware module.

## MESI

The classic simplified protocol assigns each participating cache-line entry one of four stable states:

| State | Valid | Dirty | Other copies? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **M**odified | yes | yes | none |
| **E**xclusive | yes | no | none |
| **S**hared | yes | no | maybe |
| **I**nvalid | no | - | - |

- **M**: this cache has the only copy and it has been written; the backing level may be stale. It must be written back (or handed over) before anyone else can read it.
- **E**: the only copy, clean. The core can write it **silently** (E → M) without telling anyone.
- **S**: clean, and other caches may have it too. A write first requires invalidating them.
- **I**: not usable; any access is a miss.

### Transitions

For this textbook snooping model, transactions are serialised and observed by the other participating caches. The table omits transient states, retries and simultaneous-request races:

- **BusRd**: "I want to read this line."
- **BusRdX**: "I want to write this line; everyone else invalidate" (a read-for-ownership).
- **BusUpgr**: "I already have it in S; everyone else invalidate."

| Now | Event | Action | Next |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | local read | BusRd | E (no sharers) or S |
| I | local write | BusRdX | M |
| S | local write | BusUpgr | M |
| E | local write | none | M |
| M | snoop BusRd | supply data | S |
| M | snoop BusRdX | supply data | I |
| E | snoop BusRd | - | S |
| E/S | snoop BusRdX/Upgr | - | I |

In this textbook MESI model, M → S also updates the backing level so shared copies are clean relative to it. That backing level can be another cache; a real transaction need not reach DRAM.

### Worked trace

Two cores, line X not cached anywhere.

```
 step            core0  core1  traffic
 0 read  X       E      I      BusRd
 1 read  X       S      S      BusRd
 0 write X       M      I      BusUpgr
 1 read  X       S      S      BusRd,
                                c0 supplies
 1 write X       I      M      BusUpgr
```

1. Core 0 reads: nobody else has it, so **E**.
2. Core 1 reads: core 0 sees the BusRd and drops to **S**; both S.
3. Core 0 writes: it must invalidate core 1 (BusUpgr). Core 0 **M**, core 1 **I**.
4. Core 1 reads: miss. Core 0 snoops, supplies the dirty data (and updates the backing level in this model), and both end in **S**.
5. Core 1 writes: invalidates core 0; core 1 **M**.

When a different core acquires write permission, coherence communication is required; data need not always be transferred directly from the previous writer. That is the cost to keep in mind.

### Why E exists

Without E (the simpler MSI protocol), a single-threaded program that reads then writes private data would pay two requests: BusRd to get it in S, then BusUpgr to write. E recognises "nobody else has this" and avoids a separate ownership-upgrade transaction for that write. The store still has local execution cost; how often this helps is workload-dependent.

## Variants used in real chips

- **MOESI**, used in some processor coherence designs: adds an **Owned (O) state**: dirty but shared. A core in M that is snooped by a reader moves to O and keeps supplying the data, while retaining responsibility for the dirty data. This can defer a backing-level write-back for read-shared dirty data.
- **MESIF**, used in some processor coherence designs: adds a **Forward (F) state**: among several S copies, one is designated F and is the one that answers requests, so a read gets one response rather than many.
- Arm's AMBA CHI interconnects use their own state names with equivalent ideas (unique/shared, clean/dirty).

## Snooping vs directories

How does a write find all the copies it must invalidate?

- **Snooping**: every request is broadcast and every cache checks its tags. Simple and fast with a few cores on a shared bus, but broadcast traffic grows with core count.
- **Directory**: a structure (often alongside the L3 or memory controller) tracks actual or possible sharers of a line. A write can target those candidates instead of broadcasting to every cache. Scales to many cores and CPU sockets.

Modern many-core chips mix the two: **snoop filters** (Intel) and directory caches track which cores *might* hold a line, so most requests avoid broadcasting. An inclusive L3 can act as a natural snoop filter: if a line is absent from that inclusive L3, it cannot be resident in the upper caches covered by the inclusion guarantee.

## What coherence costs

A **coherence miss** is a miss caused by a coherence invalidation of a previously cached line. A first-ever access can also obtain dirty data from another core, but that fact alone does not make it an invalidation-caused miss.

Remote ownership/data transfers can be much slower than a local L1 hit. A representative nanosecond range is absent because processor topology, load, placement and measurement method have not been reliably specified here. Measure the target system rather than treating a universal range as a guarantee.

Read-only shared lines can produce local hits after warming and while resident; initial fills, evictions and replication still consume resources. Repeated writes by different cores are a particularly costly pattern because they require ownership changes.



## False sharing

Coherence works on **lines**, not variables. If two threads write two *different* variables that happen to sit in the **same line**, the hardware treats it exactly like a contended write to one variable: the line ping-pongs between their caches in M state.

```c
#include <pthread.h>
#include <stdalign.h>
#define ITERS 100000000L

alignas(64) struct {
    volatile long a, b;
} counters;
// Assume 8-byte longs, 64-byte lines.

void *inc_a(void *_) {
    for (long i = 0; i < ITERS; i++)
        counters.a++;
    return 0;
}
void *inc_b(void *_) {
    for (long i = 0; i < ITERS; i++)
        counters.b++;
    return 0;
}
```

`volatile` requires observable accesses according to the C implementation; it is **not** an atomic or thread-synchronisation mechanism. This example has one writer per distinct scalar object; read the final counts only after joining both threads. A shared counter written by both threads would need atomics or a lock.

Each store requires ownership, but a core may execute many increments before ownership changes. The following is one possible interleaving, not one transfer guaranteed per increment:



```
 core0: write a -> needs M -> invalidate c1
 core1: write b -> needs M -> invalidate c0
 core0: write a -> miss, fetch from c1 ...
```

False sharing can make the two-core run slower; the size of the effect requires measurement. Under this 64-byte-line model, separate the independently written variables:

```c
#include <stdalign.h>
struct padded {
    alignas(64) volatile long v;
};  /* 64 bytes under the stated ABI */
struct padded counters[2];
```

### Padding in practice

- **C++17**: `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size` (where the library provides it) provides an implementation-defined separation hint, not a runtime measurement of every machine on which the binary may run.
- **Linux kernel**: `____cacheline_aligned_in_smp`.
- **Java**: `@Contended` (internal; user code needs `-XX:-RestrictContended`). `LongAdder` uses striped cells to reduce update contention; its `sum()` is not an atomic snapshot, and performance depends on contention and usage.
- **Rust**: `crossbeam_utils::CachePadded` documents a conservative **128-byte** padding choice on x86-64, including concern about adjacent-line prefetching on some processors. This library heuristic is not proof that every x86 CPU requires 128 bytes or every other platform has the same line size.
- **Go**: `golang.org/x/sys/cpu.CacheLinePad`.

### Better than padding: don't share writes

Padding fixes *false* sharing. *True* sharing (many threads updating one counter) still ping-pongs. The real fix is structural:

- Give each thread a **private accumulator** and combine at the end.
- Use **sharded/striped** counters (like `LongAdder`) when approximate concurrent aggregation is acceptable; cells are not necessarily one per thread, and a concurrent sum need not be a single-time snapshot.
- Batch updates, e.g. publish every 1,000 local events, accepting delayed visibility and flushing remaining events before a final total.

### Finding it

False sharing does not show up in source code review easily. Tools:

- `perf c2c` on Linux reports cache lines with heavy cross-core "HITM" traffic (loads that hit a modified line in another core) and the offsets within the line being touched.
- A tell-tale sign: performance gets **worse** as you add threads, while CPU utilisation stays high.

## Spinlocks and coherence

A naive spinlock repeatedly performs an atomic exchange. Under contention, competing read-modify-write requests can repeatedly transfer exclusive ownership. An exchange by a core that already owns the line need not cause a fresh transfer.

**Test-and-test-and-set** first spins on an **atomic relaxed load**, then tries an acquire exchange when the lock appears free; unlocking uses a release store. An ordinary non-atomic C/C++ load racing with a write is invalid, even on coherent hardware. Read polling can hit locally while the line remains shared, but it still reacts to invalidations.

Queue locks such as MCS let each waiter poll its own node; laying out nodes to avoid false sharing preserves that advantage. This is a protocol overview, not a complete lock implementation.



## Key takeaways
- Coherence enforces single-writer/multiple-reader per line; writes invalidate all other copies.
- MESI: M (only, dirty), E (only, clean, silent write), S (clean, shared), I. MOESI adds Owned; MESIF adds Forward.
- Snooping broadcasts; directories and snoop filters track sharers to scale.
- Ownership changes and remote data transfers can be expensive; their latency is topology- and workload-dependent.
- False sharing occurs when independent writes contend for one coherence line. Use target-appropriate layout or private accumulation, and measure the effect.

A write needs exclusive ownership. Check each state:

| State | Others have it? | Write needs |

| M | no | nothing |
| E | no | nothing (→ M) |
| S | maybe | BusUpgr |
| I | ? | BusRdX |

questions.prompt: Two pinned threads each increment their own eight-byte long counter, both confirmed in one aligned 64-byte line. Final values are read only after join. With other costs controlled, what mechanism can make the two-core run slower?

options.text: A data race corrupts the counters
options.explanation: Each thread writes only its own variable, so there's no race on the values. The problem is performance, not correctness.

options.text: False sharing: ownership of the common line can move between the two cores
options.explanation: Correct. Distinct scalar objects can still occupy one coherence line. A core can perform several stores before ownership changes, so not every increment implies a transfer.

options.text: The cores are throttled to run at a lower frequency
options.explanation: Frequency changes can affect real measurements, but the question controls other costs and asks about the demonstrated same-line layout.

options.text: The struct is too large to fit in L1
options.explanation: Under the stipulated ABI the two longs occupy 16 bytes; total cache capacity is not the relevant issue.

questions.workedExample: With the struct aligned to 64 bytes and eight-byte longs at offsets 0 and 8, both counters share a line. Each core needs write permission, so alternating ownership can invalidate the other cache. This is a possible costly pattern, not one transfer per increment. Separate independently written objects by the target coherence-line size, or accumulate privately and combine after synchronisation.

questions.prompt: Eight threads repeatedly read an immutable table. After warm-up, assume all required lines remain in each core's cache, with no evictions or invalidations. What additional coherence traffic do these reads need in textbook MESI?

options.text: Each read invalidates the other cores' copies, so it's very slow
options.explanation: A local hit on a Shared line does not require invalidating other readers.

options.text: None for the stipulated resident Shared hits: each core reads its local copy
options.explanation: Correct under the stated residency assumptions. Initial fills and later evictions or invalidations are separate costs.

options.text: The lines must be written back to memory after each read
options.explanation: Clean S lines never need write-backs.

options.text: Only one core at a time can cache a line, so the threads take turns
options.explanation: That's the rule for *writable* (M/E) lines. Any number of caches can share a line in S.

questions.workedExample: Initial readers obtain copies, transitioning exclusive copies to Shared where needed. Once each required Shared line is resident, these local read hits need no coherence transaction. Real read-only sharing still costs initial replication and may suffer replacement misses; writes are not the only possible source of later traffic.

questions.prompt: Three cores, MESI, line X initially uncached. Sequence: core 0 reads X; core 1 reads X; core 2 writes X; core 0 reads X. What are the final states in cores 0, 1 and 2? Use the lesson's textbook stable-state protocol with serialised transactions and no eviction or intervening accesses.

options.text: S, S, S
options.explanation: Core 1's copy was invalidated by core 2's write and core 1 hasn't read again, so it stays I.

options.text: E, I, I
options.explanation: Core 2 has a copy (it supplied the data), so core 0 can't be the only holder.

options.text: S, I, S
options.explanation: Correct. Core 2's write invalidated cores 0 and 1. Core 0's read then hits core 2's M copy, which is supplied and downgraded to S.

options.text: S, I, M
options.explanation: Core 2 can't stay in M once another cache holds a copy; a snooped read moves M to S (in MESI).

questions.workedExample:
Track each core (c0, c1, c2):

```
start            I  I  I
c0 read  BusRd   E  I  I
c1 read  BusRd   S  S  I
c2 write BusRdX  I  I  M
c0 read  BusRd   S  I  S
          (c2 supplies,
           writes back)
```

Final: **c0 S, c1 I, c2 S**.

questions.prompt: A single thread reads a private variable and then writes it (the line is not cached anywhere). How many coherence requests does that cost under MSI versus MESI? Use the lesson's textbook stable-state protocol with serialised transactions and no eviction or intervening accesses.

options.text: MSI 2, MESI 1
options.explanation: Correct. MSI: BusRd brings it in S, then BusUpgr to get M. MESI: BusRd brings it in E (no sharers), and the write is a silent E → M.

options.text: MSI 1, MESI 1
options.explanation: MSI has no E state, so the read can only leave the line in S, and writing from S requires an upgrade.

options.text: MSI 1, MESI 2
options.explanation: Reversed. E is what saves the second request.

options.text: MSI 2, MESI 2
options.explanation: MESI's E state exists to avoid the second request when no one else has the line.

questions.workedExample:
1. MSI: read miss → BusRd → **S** (there is no Exclusive state). Write → BusUpgr → M. **2** requests.
2. MESI: read miss → BusRd → no sharers respond → **E**. Write → E → M with no request. **1** request.
3. E avoids one of two requests for this specific cold read-then-write pattern. The overall saving depends on the workload.

questions.prompt: Each of 8 threads updates `long counts[8]` at index `tid`. Assume eight-byte longs, 64-byte coherence lines, and 64-byte alignment for both the original and replacement storage. How many cache lines does it span, and what's a correct fix for false sharing?

options.text: 8 lines; no fix needed
options.explanation: 8 × 8 bytes = 64 bytes, which is *one* line, not eight.

options.text: 1 line; use `counts[tid * 8]` in a 64-element array, or a struct padded to 64 bytes per thread
options.explanation: Correct. All 8 counters share one line, so all 8 threads fight over it. Spreading them 64 bytes apart gives each its own line.

options.text: 1 line; make the array `volatile`
options.explanation: `volatile` specifies observable accesses, but provides neither atomicity nor thread synchronisation. It doesn't move the counters to different lines, so false sharing remains.

options.text: 2 lines; split it into two arrays of 4
options.explanation: Two arrays of 4 counters still put 4 writers on each line.

questions.workedExample:
1. Work out the array size, then how many 64-byte lines it covers. Because the array starts on a 64-byte boundary, no line is only partly used:

```formula
S_arr = n × s_long
S_arr = 8 × 8 B = 64 B
N_lines = S_arr / B_line
N_lines = 64 B / 64 B = 1
where
S_arr: the total size of the array, in bytes (B)
n: the number of counters, one per thread: 8
s_long: the size of one long, 8 bytes under the stated ABI
N_lines: how many cache lines the array occupies
B_line: the coherence (cache line) size, 64 bytes
B: byte, 8 bits
In words: eight 8-byte counters fill exactly one 64-byte line, so every thread writes the same line.
```

2. Every thread's write needs that line in M, so it ping-pongs among 8 cores.
3. Fix: give each counter its own line:

```
struct slot {
  alignas(64) long v;
};
struct slot counts[8];
```

   Now `sizeof(counts) = 512` bytes, 8 lines, one per thread.
4. Better still: count in a local variable and write once at the end.

questions.prompt: Which statements about snooping and directory coherence are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: In snooping, every cache observes every coherence request and checks its own tags
options.explanation: Correct. That's the definition: requests are broadcast, and each cache reacts if it holds the line.

options.text: A directory tracks actual or possible sharers, allowing targeted invalidations
options.explanation: Correct. Some directories use conservative representations and may contact extra candidates; exact sharer lists are not required.

options.text: Snooping scales better than directories as the core count grows
options.explanation: Broadcast traffic and tag-check bandwidth grow with core count; directories scale better.

options.text: An L3 inclusive of specified private caches can filter snoops: a missing L3 line is absent from those caches
options.explanation: Correct for the caches covered by the inclusion guarantee; it is not a statement about every cache or device in the machine.

options.text: Directory protocols remove the need for invalidations
options.explanation: They still invalidate; they just know *whom* to send the invalidations to.

questions.workedExample:
- Snooping: requests are broadcast and every cache checks its tags. ✔
- Directory: tracks the sharers and sends targeted messages. ✔
- Snooping scaling better: no; broadcasts grow with cores. ✘
- Inclusive L3 as filter: yes, a common trick. ✔
- Directories still invalidate, they're just targeted. ✘

Real many-core chips combine both: snoop filters or directory caches decide when a broadcast is needed.

questions.prompt: In textbook MESI versus MOESI, a producer holds a Modified line and another core reads it. What can the Owned state avoid at that transition?

options.text: Nothing; MOESI and MESI behave identically here
options.explanation: They differ exactly here: what happens to a Modified line when another core reads it.

options.text: An immediate update of the backing level: the producer can retain dirty-data responsibility in Owned
options.explanation: Correct. MESI sharing requires a clean backing copy in this model; MOESI can retain a dirty shared owner. Later write-back or ownership transfer depends on subsequent events.

options.text: The invalidation of the consumers' copies on the next write
options.explanation: The next producer write must still invalidate the three S copies; Owned doesn't change that.

options.text: The consumers' cache misses, because MOESI pushes updates to them
options.explanation: The reader still needs the data. Adding Owned does not turn a write-invalidate protocol into a write-update protocol.

questions.workedExample: Textbook MESI: the producer supplies the read and updates the backing level, then both hold Shared. MOESI: the producer can become Owned and supply the reader without updating the backing level at that moment. The backing level may be another cache, not DRAM. Eviction is not the only later event that can propagate data or transfer responsibility, so no universal million-write DRAM-traffic saving follows.

questions.prompt: Crossbeam documents a conservative 128-byte CachePadded alignment on x86-64. On a model machine with 64-byte coherence lines and adjacent-pair prefetching, what concern motivates padding beyond one line?

options.text: x86-64 cache lines are 128 bytes
options.explanation: The stipulated machine has 64-byte lines. Padding can be chosen larger than coherence granularity without claiming every x86-64 processor has one particular geometry.

options.text: A spatial prefetcher may fetch the neighbouring line in a 128-byte-aligned pair
options.explanation: Correct. Crossbeam cites adjacent-line prefetching as one motivation for conservative padding. The behaviour and benefit depend on the processor and workload.

options.text: `alignas(64)` is ignored by compilers on x86
options.explanation: Compilers honour `alignas(64)`; the alignment does take effect.

options.text: Padding must equal the L1 size per way
options.explanation: Cache capacity per way is not the coherence-line or adjacent-prefetch-pair size in this model.

questions.workedExample: If a prefetcher brings both halves of an aligned 128-byte region into a cache, a neighbour's independently written line may be fetched unnecessarily and later invalidated. Placing counters in separate 128-byte regions can avoid that particular interaction. This is a documented library heuristic, not proof that every observed contention event has this cause or every x86 processor needs that padding.

questions.prompt: Threads contend on a C/C++ atomic spinlock. Test-and-test-and-set polls with atomic relaxed loads, attempts an acquire exchange when free, and unlocks with a release store. Why can that reduce traffic compared with continuously exchanging?

options.text: Loads are atomic and exchanges are not
options.explanation: Both specified operations are atomic. Ordinary non-atomic loads are not made safe against racing writes merely by alignment or hardware coherence.

options.text: Read polling can hit in shared copies, avoiding repeated competing ownership requests while the lock is held
options.explanation: Correct. A read-modify-write needs exclusive permission, whereas a resident shared read can hit locally. Not every exchange causes a new transfer if the caller already owns the line.

options.text: The exchange instruction disables the cache
options.explanation: An atomic exchange does not generally disable caching. Ordinary aligned operations on cacheable memory can use coherence; special split or uncacheable cases have additional rules.

options.text: TTAS reduces the critical section length
options.explanation: The critical section is unchanged; what changes is the coherence traffic while waiting.

questions.workedExample: Continuous competing exchanges can repeatedly demand ownership. Atomic read polling can instead use Shared hits while the value stays unchanged. Release updates invalidate those copies; contenders then attempt acquisition, potentially causing a burst of traffic. MCS-style queue locks let each waiter poll a distinct node; suitable layout avoids false sharing between nodes. The language-level atomic operations remain necessary.

questions.prompt: Many threads increment one global AtomicLong statistic. Approximate concurrent snapshots and delayed batched visibility are acceptable, with exact final totals after synchronised completion. Which changes can reduce update contention? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pad `requests` to its own 64- or 128-byte line
options.explanation: This is *true* sharing: one variable, many writers. Padding only helps when *different* variables share a line.

options.text: Use a striped counter such as LongAdder, distributing updates over cells
options.explanation: Correct. Cells are not necessarily one per thread; this can reduce contention. sum() is not an atomic snapshot during concurrent updates.

options.text: Keep a per-thread count and add it to the global counter every 1,000 requests
options.explanation: Correct. Batch publication reduces shared updates; flush each remainder before the final total. It changes when requests become visible.

options.text: Switch from `AtomicLong.incrementAndGet()` to a `synchronized` block
options.explanation: A lock adds its own shared, written lock word. The line still bounces, now with lock overhead on top.

options.text: Use suitably separated per-thread counters with atomic reads or synchronised aggregation
options.explanation: Correct. Distinct writers reduce update contention; concurrent metrics readers still need safe atomic or synchronised access.

questions.workedExample: This is true sharing of one counter. Padding alone cannot remove that contention, though it can prevent unrelated false sharing. Striping, batching, or separate safely read counters distribute writes. These approaches change snapshot/visibility semantics, so use them only when the statistic permits that trade-off. Read exact final totals after updates stop and all remainders are published.

lessons.title: DRAM, NUMA and prefetching
lessons.summary: What happens below the last-level cache - DRAM cells, banks and row buffers, timings and bandwidth maths, refresh, NUMA on multi-socket machines, and how hardware and software prefetching hide memory latency.
lessons.body:
Earlier examples used assumed DRAM latencies to explain cache arithmetic. Below the last-level cache is a memory system with controllers, channels, ranks, banks and rows. Access latency depends on its state, traffic and placement. Streaming throughput benefits from overlapping requests, including useful prefetches; it is not guaranteed to reach peak bandwidth.

The numerical examples below are explicit models. Representative end-to-end latency and speedup figures are absent where the necessary processor, memory configuration and benchmark have not been reliably verified.



## The DRAM cell and why it is slow

A conventional DRAM cell uses **one transistor and one capacitor**. Information is represented by charge state; the mapping of charged/discharged to logical 1/0 can depend on cell organisation. That makes DRAM dense and cheap, but it has three consequences:

- **Reads are destructive.** Activation shares the cell's small charge with a bit line. A **sense amplifier** resolves the voltage difference and restores the cell while the row is active. This disturbs the stored charge; it is not simply a complete drain followed by restoration during precharge.
- **Cells leak.** Charge drains away in milliseconds, so every row must be **refreshed** (read and rewritten) periodically, whether or not anyone uses it.
- **Access is row-at-a-time.** The chip cannot read one bit cheaply. It opens a whole **row** (thousands of bits) into the sense amplifiers, called the **row buffer**, and then reads columns from it.

## Inside a DIMM: channels, ranks, banks, rows

The following is an **illustrative DDR4-style topology**, excluding ECC bits; actual widths, ranks, bank counts and address mapping vary.

```
 memory controller (on the CPU)
   |-- channel 0 (64-bit bus)
   |     |-- rank 0: 8 chips side by side
   |     |     |-- bank 0 .. bank 15
   |     |     |     rows x columns
   |     |     |     + 1 row buffer
   |     |-- rank 1 ...
   |-- channel 1 ...
```

- A **memory channel** is an independent bus with its own controller logic. More channels means more bandwidth in parallel.
- A **DRAM rank** groups DRAM devices operated together. In the illustrated 64-data-bit DDR4 channel, eight ×8 (8-bit-wide) devices supply the data width; ECC may add bits. DDR5 DIMMs divide their data interface into sub-channels.
- Each chip has several **DRAM banks**, with counts depending on device width and generation; DDR5 configurations can have up to 32. Each bank has its own row buffer, so different banks can work on different rows at the same time.
- A **DRAM row** (sometimes called a page) is distinct from an operating-system page. Its aggregate byte size depends on device geometry and rank width; no universal row size is assumed here.

The memory controller maps, and may hash, physical address bits to choose channel, rank, bank, row and column. Consecutive cache lines are usually spread across channels and banks so that a stream keeps them all busy.

## The three cases of an access

Each bank's row buffer retains an activated row. The table gives simplified command-to-first-data minima, assuming precharge is already legal, the command bus is available, and all other timing constraints are satisfied. Queueing, transfer completion and earlier operations can add delay:

| Case | Commands | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Row hit | READ | CL |
| Row empty | ACT, READ | tRCD + CL |
| Row conflict | PRE, ACT, READ | tRP + tRCD + CL |

- **CL** (CAS latency): column read from an open row to first data.
- **tRCD**: activate a row (copy it into the row buffer).
- **tRP**: precharge time to close the row and prepare/equalise the bit lines for another activation. Cell restoration occurs while the row is active.

Timings are quoted in clock cycles, as in "DDR4-3200 CL22-22-22". To convert to nanoseconds you need the clock. DDR means **double data rate**: two transfers per clock. So DDR4-3200 runs 3,200 mega-transfers per second (MT/s) on a 1,600 MHz clock, and one clock is 0.625 ns.

To turn a timing quoted in clock cycles into nanoseconds, divide the cycles by the clock frequency. The clock is half the data-transfer rate, which is where the 2,000 comes from:

```formula
t = N_cyc × 2,000 / R
t = 22 × 2,000 / 3,200
t = 13.75 ns
where
t: the timing in nanoseconds (ns)
N_cyc: the timing in memory clock cycles, e.g. CL = 22
R: the data-transfer rate in MT/s, e.g. 3,200 for DDR4-3200
MT/s: mega-transfers per second: millions of data transfers each second
2,000: 1,000 (to turn a frequency in millions per second into nanoseconds) × 2 (two transfers per clock)
ns: nanosecond, one billionth of a second
In words: a DDR4-3200 clock tick is 2,000 / 3,200 = 0.625 ns, so 22 ticks take 13.75 ns.
```

The rule holds for any DDR generation, because all of them make two transfers per clock. It converts the quoted minimum only; real loads add queueing and other delays.

### Worked example: hit, empty, conflict

Assume a DDR4-3200 timing configuration with CL, tRCD and tRP all equal to 22 clocks, so each is 13.75 ns. Add up the steps each case needs, from the table above:

```formula
t_hit = t_CL = 13.75 ns
t_empty = t_RCD + t_CL
t_empty = 13.75 + 13.75 = 27.5 ns
t_conf = t_RP + t_RCD + t_CL
t_conf = 3 × 13.75 = 41.25 ns
where
t_hit: time to first data for a row hit, in nanoseconds (ns)
t_empty: time to first data when no row is open
t_conf: time to first data when a different row is open (a row-buffer conflict)
t_CL: the CAS latency, read from an open row: 22 cycles = 13.75 ns
t_RCD: the activate (row-to-column) delay: 22 cycles = 13.75 ns
t_RP: the precharge time to close the old row: 22 cycles = 13.75 ns
ns: nanosecond, one billionth of a second
In words: a hit pays one step, an empty bank two, and a conflict three, so here a conflict takes three times as long as a hit.
```

In this simplified example, the command-to-first-data interval for a conflict is three times the hit interval. That is why controllers reorder queued requests to group hits to the same open row (FR-FCFS scheduling), and why two streams repeatedly accessing different rows of the same bank are slow.

These are simplified DRAM command intervals. A measured core load also includes cache lookups, interconnect traversal, controller scheduling and possible contention; its latency cannot be inferred from CL alone.

> [!tip] Faster MT/s is not always lower latency
> DDR4-3200 CL16 and DDR4-3600 CL18 both work out to **10 ns** of CAS latency (calculation below). A higher CL number at a higher data-transfer rate can be the same latency, with more bandwidth.

```formula
t = N_cyc × 2,000 / R
t = 16 × 2,000 / 3,200 = 10 ns
t = 18 × 2,000 / 3,600 = 10 ns
where
t: the CAS latency in nanoseconds (ns)
N_cyc: the CAS latency in clock cycles (the CL number)
R: the data-transfer rate in MT/s
MT/s: mega-transfers per second
2,000: 1,000 (millions per second to nanoseconds) × 2 (two transfers per clock)
ns: nanosecond, one billionth of a second
In words: more cycles at a proportionally faster clock take the same time.
```

## Bandwidth maths

The most data a channel can ever move is one bus-width of bytes per transfer, times the number of transfers each second:

```formula
BW = R × W_bus
BW = 3,200 M/s × 8 B
BW = 25,600 MB/s = 25.6 GB/s
BW_2 = 2 × 25.6 = 51.2 GB/s
where
BW: peak bandwidth of one channel, in gigabytes per second (GB/s)
R: the data-transfer rate; DDR4-3200 makes 3,200 million (M) transfers per second
W_bus: the bus width in bytes; a 64-bit channel moves 8 bytes (B) per transfer
BW_2: peak bandwidth of two channels (dual channel)
M: mega, a million
B: byte, 8 bits
MB/s: megabytes (millions of bytes) per second
GB/s: gigabytes per second; here GB is 10^9 bytes, as memory vendors use
In words: 3.2 billion transfers a second of 8 bytes each is 25.6 GB/s; a second channel doubles it.
```

This is a ceiling: refresh, row-buffer conflicts, bus turnarounds and too few requests in flight keep real programs below it. A 64-byte line is one **DRAM burst** of 8 transfers of 8 bytes (BL8). Two transfers happen per clock, so that is 4 clocks of 0.625 ns, or 2.5 ns of bus time on DDR4-3200.

A conventional **DDR5 DIMM** splits its 64-bit data interface into **two independent 32-bit sub-channels**, excluding additional ECC bits, each using bursts of 16 (BL16 × 4 B = 64 B, still one line). Two narrower channels give the controller more parallelism.

The same peak-bandwidth formula applies, counting both sub-channels together as 8 bytes per transfer:

```formula
BW = R × W_bus
BW = 4,800 M/s × 8 B = 38.4 GB/s
BW_s = N_ch × BW
BW_s = 12 × 38.4 = 460.8 GB/s
where
BW: peak bandwidth of one DDR5-4800 DIMM channel, in GB/s
R: the data-transfer rate, 4,800 million (M) transfers per second
W_bus: bytes per transfer across both 32-bit sub-channels: 8 bytes (B)
BW_s: peak bandwidth of the whole CPU socket
N_ch: the number of memory channels, 12 in this hypothetical CPU socket
M: mega, a million
B: byte, 8 bits
GB/s: gigabytes (10^9 bytes) per second
In words: one DDR5-4800 DIMM peaks at 38.4 GB/s, and twelve channels at 460.8 GB/s.
```

DDR5 devices add on-die ECC, while conventional DDR5 DIMMs include on-module power management; bank counts depend on device geometry. On-die ECC protects internal storage and does not replace end-to-end memory-system ECC. For the **example** DDR5-4800 CL40, CAS latency is about 16.7 ns (40 × 2,000 / 4,800, using the conversion formula above) versus the example DDR4-3200 CL22's 13.75 ns. These two configurations do not establish a universal latency ordering between generations.

## Little's law: requests in flight

Peak bandwidth is only reached if enough requests are **in flight** at once. Little's law, from queueing theory, says that in a steady state the number of items inside a system equals the rate they flow through it times how long each stays. Rearranged for memory:

```formula
BW = Q / L
Q = N_req × B_line
where
BW: the sustained bandwidth, in bytes per nanosecond (B/ns); 1 B/ns = 1 GB/s
Q: bytes in flight: data requested but not yet returned, in bytes (B)
N_req: the number of outstanding requests
B_line: bytes per request, 64 for one cache line
L: the average time each request stays outstanding (its latency), in nanoseconds (ns)
B: byte, 8 bits
ns: nanosecond, one billionth of a second
GB/s: gigabytes (10^9 bytes) per second
In words: you can only receive as many bytes per nanosecond as you have waiting, divided by how long each wait lasts.
```

It applies to averages over a steady period, not to single requests. As an illustrative demand-request limit, assume 12 outstanding 64-byte transfers with a steady-state average residency of 80 ns:

```formula
Q = 12 × 64 B = 768 B
BW = 768 B / 80 ns = 9.6 B/ns
BW = 9.6 GB/s
where
Q: bytes in flight, in bytes (B)
BW: the sustained bandwidth
B/ns: bytes per nanosecond, the same as GB/s
B: byte, 8 bits
ns: nanosecond
GB/s: gigabytes (10^9 bytes) per second
In words: twelve 64-byte requests, each taking 80 ns, deliver at most 9.6 GB/s.
```

Turned round, the law says how many requests a target bandwidth needs:

```formula
Q = BW × L
Q = 51.2 B/ns × 80 ns = 4,096 B
N_req = 4,096 B / 64 B = 64
where
Q: bytes that must be in flight, in bytes (B)
BW: the target bandwidth: 51.2 GB/s = 51.2 B/ns (dual-channel DDR4-3200)
L: the average request latency, 80 ns
N_req: the number of 64-byte line requests outstanding
B/ns: bytes per nanosecond, the same as GB/s
B: byte, 8 bits
ns: nanosecond
In words: to fill 51.2 GB/s at 80 ns per request you need 64 lines in flight at all times.
```

So at 51.2 GB/s and an 80 ns average request residency you need **64 lines in flight**. The hypothetical 12-request limit cannot sustain that rate by itself. Actual limits and prefetch queues are implementation-specific. One strictly dependent cold pointer chain can expose only one next demand address at a time: with the assumed 80 ns per line, it moves one 64-byte line per 80 ns, which is 0.8 GB/s of line traffic. Useful pointer-byte throughput is lower, and other chains or hardware speculation can create additional requests.

## Refresh

DRAM retention requires periodic refresh; the interval, blocking time, temperature rules and supported modes are part-specific. For an **illustrative all-bank refresh model**, assume one operation every 7,812.5 ns, blocking the rank for 350 ns. The share of time lost is the blocked time divided by the interval:

```formula
f_ref = t_RFC / t_REFI
f_ref = 350 ns / 7,812.5 ns
f_ref ≈ 0.0448 = 4.48%
where
f_ref: the fraction of time the rank is busy refreshing
t_RFC: how long one refresh blocks the rank, 350 nanoseconds (ns) here
t_REFI: the interval between refresh operations, 7,812.5 ns here
≈: approximately equal to
%: per cent, parts per hundred
ns: nanosecond, one billionth of a second
In words: blocking for 350 ns out of every 7,812.5 ns loses about 4.5% of the rank's time.
```

If that interval halves while the blocking duration stays fixed, the fraction doubles to 8.96%. A product-specific density/temperature timing table is absent because those exact operating modes have not been reliably verified here.

DDR5 **same-bank refresh** targets one selected bank **in each bank group**, allowing other banks to remain available subject to timing constraints. It is not a refresh of only one bank in the entire device. A demand request can still be delayed by refresh.



> [!warning] Row hammer
> Activating one row very rapidly can disturb the charge in *neighbouring* rows and flip their bits, faster than refresh restores them. Researchers have used this to escalate privileges from unprivileged code. Mitigations include target row refresh (TRR) in the DRAM, DDR5's refresh management, and ECC, but none is perfect.

## NUMA: not all DRAM is equally far

In a multi-socket server, each CPU socket has its own memory controllers and DRAM. A core can reach the other CPU socket's memory, but only over the inter-socket link (Intel UPI, AMD Infinity Fabric). This is **non-uniform memory access**.

```
 +---------+   UPI    +---------+
 | socket0 |<-------->| socket1 |
 | cores   |          | cores   |
 | MC      |          | MC      |
 +----+----+          +----+----+
      |                    |
   node 0 DRAM          node 1 DRAM
   local memory        remote memory
```

Remote access can add interconnect delay and encounter link-bandwidth limits. A universal local/remote latency ratio is absent because a specific measured topology is not established here. `numactl --hardware` reports node memory and relative distance values; these are not nanoseconds. A CPU socket can expose multiple NUMA nodes, and a NUMA node need not correspond one-to-one with a CPU socket.



### Worked example: average latency

For a hypothetical workload with local 90 ns, remote 140 ns, and a quarter of accesses remote:

The average is a weighted mix: each latency counts in proportion to how often it happens.

```formula
L_avg = (1 − p) × L_loc + p × L_rem
L_avg = 0.75 × 90 + 0.25 × 140
L_avg = 67.5 + 35 = 102.5 ns
where
L_avg: the average memory latency, in nanoseconds (ns)
p: the fraction of accesses that go to remote memory; here 0.25
L_loc: the latency of a local-memory access, 90 ns
L_rem: the latency of a remote-memory access, 140 ns
ns: nanosecond, one billionth of a second
In words: three quarters of accesses at 90 ns and one quarter at 140 ns average 102.5 ns.
```

If all were remote: 140 ns, which is 140 / 90 ≈ 1.56 times the all-local figure, or 56% worse. The model assumes fixed latencies; in reality remote latency rises when the inter-socket link is busy.

### First touch

Under Linux's default local allocation policy, a newly faulted writable anonymous page is normally allocated near the CPU taking the fault, subject to allowed nodes, free memory and fallback. `malloc` may return **already backed** reused storage, so calling or writing through it does not necessarily cause a new allocation. Placement can also change through migration or automatic NUMA balancing. For the following example, assume fresh untouched pages, a pinned initialising thread, sufficient local memory, and no policy override or migration:

```c
double *a = malloc(n * sizeof *a);
for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++)
    a[i] = 0.0;   /* main thread */
/* ...then 64 threads on 2 sockets
   each process a slice of a[] */
```

Under those assumptions, initial page faults place the pages on the main thread's node. Workers on another node then reach remote memory when accesses miss the cache hierarchy; hits in a core's own caches are not remote DRAM accesses.

Fixes:

- **Parallel first touch**: initialise newly allocated, unbacked slices with the workers that will later process them, pinned appropriately. Re-zeroing already placed pages does not by itself relocate them.
- **Pin** threads and memory: `numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 ./app`, or `taskset` plus `mbind`/`set_mempolicy` from libnuma.
- **Interleave**: `numactl --interleave=all` spreads pages round-robin. This can balance placement for large shared structures, but does not guarantee equal access latency or eliminate bandwidth hotspots.
- **Automatic NUMA balancing** (`kernel.numa_balancing`) migrates pages towards the threads that use them, at the cost of page faults to sample accesses.

Some database and managed-runtime configurations expose NUMA options. Collector/version-specific JVM behaviour is not detailed here because the necessary configuration-specific verification is unavailable.

## Prefetching: hiding the latency

A prefetch fetches a line **before** the demand load asks for it. Done well, a 100 ns miss becomes an L1 or L2 hit.

### Hardware prefetchers

Depending on the processor, engines may detect adjacent lines, sequential streams or constant strides associated with a load instruction. Their triggering, how far ahead they run, target cache and page-crossing behaviour vary.

Conventional stream/stride predictors struggle with irregular indirection. However, it is false that **all** hardware prefetchers are unable to use indirect data: Intel documents a **data-dependent prefetcher** that can use loaded values to predict addresses in supported patterns. That feature is not an unrestricted recursive pointer-chasing engine. Likewise, a universal “all prefetchers stop at 4 KiB boundaries” rule is incorrect; translation and boundary handling are engine-specific.



### Software prefetching

For irregular but *computable* addresses, you can issue the prefetch yourself. GCC and Clang provide `__builtin_prefetch`:

```c
#define D 16  /* prefetch distance */
for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (n - i > D)
        __builtin_prefetch(
            &table[idx[i + D]]);
    sum += table[idx[i]];
}
```

Assume every index used here is in bounds for `table`, `idx` contains at least n entries, and sum arithmetic is valid. A prefetch hint may be ignored, but evaluating its address must still be valid.

The prefetch must be issued early enough that the data arrives by the time the loop reaches it. With a constant cost per iteration, an initial **prefetch-distance estimate** is:

```formula
D = ⌈L_mem / t_iter⌉
D = ⌈100 ns / 5 ns⌉ = 20
where
D: the prefetch distance: how many iterations ahead to prefetch
L_mem: the memory latency to hide, in nanoseconds (ns); 100 ns assumed
t_iter: the time one loop iteration takes, in ns; 5 ns assumed
⌈ ⌉: ceiling: round up to the next whole number
ns: nanosecond, one billionth of a second
In words: if a miss takes as long as 20 iterations, ask for the data 20 iterations before you need it.
```

With assumed 100 ns latency and 5 ns per iteration, D = 20 is a starting estimate. Actual latency, issue overhead, resource limits and evictions determine whether it hides the miss. Too small and the data arrives late; too large and it may be evicted before use, or waste fill buffers.

### When prefetching hurts

- **Cache pollution**: prefetched lines that are never used evict useful ones.
- **Bandwidth waste**: on a memory-bound multi-threaded workload, useless prefetches steal bandwidth from demand misses. That is why BIOS settings let you switch individual prefetchers off, and some HPC sites do.
- **Overhead**: software prefetches are instructions too; in a loop that is already compute-bound they only cost.

## Putting it together

Some practical consequences:

- A sufficiently concurrent **streaming** loop can become bandwidth-limited. Too few outstanding requests or substantial computation can prevent this. Measure achieved GB/s.
- A strictly dependent, cache-missing **pointer chain** is often latency-limited: one next demand address at a time. Restructure the data (arrays, B-trees), or interleave several independent chases so their misses overlap.
- On **multi-socket** machines, check `numastat` and placement before blaming the code.
- **Bandwidth is shared.** Several cores streaming at once saturate the channels long before they saturate the cores; adding threads to a memory-bound loop stops helping once DRAM is full.

## Key takeaways
- Conventional DRAM activates a row into sense amplifiers. With other constraints already satisfied, simplified first-data intervals are CL, tRCD + CL, or tRP + tRCD + CL.
- Convert timings to nanoseconds by multiplying the cycle count by 2,000 and dividing by the MT/s rating; DDR4-3200 CL22 is 13.75 ns.
- A 64-bit channel's peak bandwidth is its MT/s rating times 8 bytes (25.6 GB/s for DDR4-3200); reaching it needs many misses in flight (Little's law).
- Refresh blocks affected resources for part-specific intervals and can delay demand requests.
- NUMA placement matters when reaching DRAM. Under suitable allocation/policy conditions, parallel first touch can place fresh pages near their users; verify actual placement.
- Prefetch capabilities vary. A software prefetch distance of roughly the memory latency divided by the iteration time is an initial model, and safe address evaluation remains required.

```formula
where
```

```formula
N = 22 + 22 + 22 = 66 cycles
t_c = 1,000 / f_clk

t_RCD: activate delay (open new row): 22 cycles
```

questions.prompt: In a hypothetical steady-state model, a core tracks at most 12 demand transfers, each 64 bytes, with average request residency 80 ns. Using Little's law, what is the most bandwidth that core's demand misses can sustain?

options.text: 0.8 GB/s
options.explanation: That's one miss in flight (64 B / 80 ns), the pointer-chasing case. With 12 independent misses, they overlap.

options.text: 9.6 GB/s
options.explanation: Correct. 12 × 64 B = 768 B in flight; 768 B / 80 ns = 9.6 B/ns = 9.6 GB/s.
That's the channel's peak, which assumes enough requests in flight to keep it busy. 12 misses at 80 ns can't do that.
This multiplies the bytes in flight by the latency (768 × 80 = 61,440) instead of dividing. Bandwidth is bytes in flight divided by latency.

questions.workedExample:
Little's law: in a steady state, throughput is the amount in flight divided by how long each item stays.

```formula
Q = N_req × B_line
Q = 12 × 64 B = 768 B
BW = Q / L
BW = 768 B / 80 ns = 9.6 B/ns
BW = 9.6 GB/s
where
Q: bytes in flight (requested, not yet returned)
N_req: outstanding requests, at most 12
B_line: bytes per request, 64
BW: sustained bandwidth
L: average request latency, 80 nanoseconds (ns)
B/ns: bytes per nanosecond; equal to GB/s
B: byte, 8 bits
ns: nanosecond, one billionth of a second
GB/s: gigabytes (10^9 bytes) per second
In words: 768 bytes outstanding, each wait lasting 80 ns, sustains 9.6 GB/s.
```

To saturate a 51.2 GB/s dual-channel system you'd need 51.2 B/ns × 80 ns = 4,096 bytes in flight, which is 4,096 / 64 = 64 lines. The hypothetical 12-request demand path alone is insufficient. Additional concurrent traffic could come from other cores or implementation-specific prefetch resources; this is not a universal statement about every core.

options.explanation: 120 ns is the simple average of 90 and 150, which assumes half the accesses are remote.

options.text: 108 ns
132 ns
options.explanation: This swaps the weights: 0.3 × 90 + 0.7 × 150 = 27 + 105 = 132 ns. Only 30% of accesses are remote, so 70% get the 90 ns local latency.

options.text: 117 ns

questions.workedExample:
Weighted average over local and remote: each latency counts in proportion to how often it happens.

```formula
L_avg = (1 − p) × L_loc + p × L_rem
L_avg = 0.7 × 90 + 0.3 × 150
L_avg = 63 + 45 = 108 ns
where
L_avg: average DRAM latency, in nanoseconds (ns)
p: fraction of accesses that are remote, 0.3
L_loc: local DRAM latency, 90 ns
L_rem: remote DRAM latency, 150 ns
ns: nanosecond, one billionth of a second
In words: 70% of accesses at 90 ns and 30% at 150 ns average 108 ns.
```

Equivalently, start from local and add the remote penalty for 30% of accesses: 90 ns plus 30% of 60 ns (18 ns) is 108 ns, 20% worse than all-local. Bandwidth can suffer more than latency, because remote traffic shares the inter-socket link.
